chunks: And as for what was narrated - Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Safwan ibn Yahya from Isḥaq ibn 'Ammar from Abū Ibrāhīm (peace be upon him) who said:

I asked him about a man who had a female slave and he married her to another man, asking 'In whose hand is her divorce?' He said, 'In the hand of her master, and that is because he married her while knowing that she is [a slave].' This also carries the meaning we mentioned earlier, that he meant by 'in his hand is her divorce' that he meant her sale, so her sale is like divorce. And it is permissible that the word 'divorce' be used metaphorically for that, because it is a cause of separation, just as divorce is. And what indicates that is what was narrated:
ai.seo_question: Who holds the right of divorce for a female slave when her master marries her off to another man?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies that a master retains the right of 'talaq' (divorce/release) over a female slave he marries off, as the act of selling her serves as the cause of separation. Al-Tusi notes the scholarly nuance that 'talaq' here may be used metaphorically for sale, reflecting the juristic view that the master’s ownership includes the authority to dissolve the marital bond by transferring her status. This highlights the distinct legal framework for *mukatab* and *umm walad* slaves in Shia fiqh, where the master’s right of disposal intersects with marital rights.
